Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly
Description: Definition: Root cause located at the user-submitted workload semantics, where application-issued statements, stored routines, or transaction boundaries are written in a way that forces the engine to process more data, more rows, or longer transactions than the business requirement actually needs. This is the highest layer of root-cause attribution and is independent of the optimizer, configuration, and hardware. Observable phenomena: long-tail statement latency reported by engine-level statement-statistics views, the same statements appearing repeatedly in slow-query logs, individual transactions holding resources for unusually long periods, application-level timeouts and retries, and session traces showing wide row scans, repeated round-trips, or oversized result sets. Possible contributing factors: predicates that are not index-friendly or that wrap indexed columns inside functions, projection of unnecessary columns, unintended Cartesian joins, sub-optimal join order written by the application, repeated single-row access patterns produced by object-relational frameworks, missing or overly broad filter conditions, oversized in-list predicates, excessive batch sizes, transactions kept open across user think-time or external service calls, and ad-hoc analytical queries running directly against transactional tables.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly
Description: Definition: Root cause located at the physical data-model layer, where table structure, partitioning strategy, indexing, integrity constraints, or column data types do not match the access patterns of the running workload, so even well-written statements are forced into inefficient access paths. It is independent of statistics freshness and plan-selection decisions and reflects a static design mismatch. Observable phenomena: execution plans dominated by full-table or full-index scans where selective lookups are expected, repeated lookups against non-covering indexes that require additional row fetches, unbalanced partition pruning, integrity-check overhead during data modifications, oversized index sets slowing down write operations, and query latency that improves substantially only after adding or restructuring an index. Possible contributing factors: missing single-column or composite indexes on frequent predicates, missing covering or filtered indexes, redundant or duplicated indexes inflating maintenance cost, inappropriate primary-key choice causing write hot-spots, missing partitioning on large time-series or multi-tenant tables, inappropriate column data types causing implicit type conversions, and absence of integrity constraints that would let the optimizer prune unreachable branches.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly
Description: Definition: Root cause located in the optimizer's input metadata, where row counts, value distribution histograms, density information, multi-column correlation, and partition-level statistics no longer represent the actual data distribution, leading to systematic cardinality misestimation. It is distinct from plan selection itself because the failure originates from incorrect costing inputs rather than from the cost model or decision logic. Observable phenomena: large discrepancies between estimated and actual row counts in execution-plan output, plans degrading immediately after bulk loads or partition exchanges, catalog views showing statistics-update timestamps lagging far behind the latest data-change timestamps, and recurrent statistics-changed or plan-recompile events. Possible contributing factors: high-velocity data modifications never crossing automatic-analysis thresholds on very large tables, automatic statistics collection disabled or rate-limited, bulk-load sessions suppressing automatic statistics maintenance, missing extended or multi-column statistics for correlated predicates, missing histograms on highly skewed columns, sampling rates too low to capture skew, and stale global statistics on partitioned tables after partition-level data changes.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly
Description: Definition: Root cause located at the optimizer's plan-selection stage, where the chosen execution plan is substantially sub-optimal due to the cost model, plan reuse, or context-dependent decisions even though the statistical inputs are reasonably accurate. It is distinct from statistics anomalies because the costing inputs are acceptable but the decision logic produces a poor plan. Observable phenomena: identical statement text producing very different plans across executions, sudden switches from selective index access to full scans, nested-loop blowouts driven by high outer-side cardinality, unexpected gain or loss of parallelism, plan changes immediately following a configuration change, version upgrade, or plan-cache invalidation, and large gaps between the cached plan cost and the actual execution cost. Possible contributing factors: bind-value-sensitive plan reuse with skewed parameter values, plan-cache pollution and excessive ad-hoc plans, optimizer version or default cost-model changes after upgrades, lack of plan-stability mechanisms such as plan baselines, stored hints, or query-fingerprint plan stores, partition-pruning failures, and cost-model parameters not aligned with the actual hardware characteristics.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly
Description: Definition: Root cause located in the lock-manager layer, where concurrent transactions request mutually incompatible row, key-range, page, table, metadata, or advisory locks on the same resource and either wait in queues or form circular wait-for cycles that the engine must break by aborting a victim transaction. This category covers both ordinary blocking chains and deadlocks because both share the lock manager as their root-cause locus. Observable phenomena: ungranted lock entries in lock-state catalogs and visible blocker-waiter chains, deadlock-detection reports and victim-rollback errors driving application retries, rising lock-wait time, declining transaction throughput, growing connection-pool wait queues, and application-level timeouts triggered by sustained blocking. Possible contributing factors: hot rows or counter columns updated by many concurrent sessions, long-running or uncommitted transactions, transactions held open across user interaction or external service calls, missing indexes that enlarge the lock footprint of a statement, overly strict transaction isolation levels, automatic lock-granularity escalation from row to page or table, online schema-change or metadata locks colliding with data modifications, and inconsistent resource-acquisition order across application code paths.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly
Description: Definition: Root cause located in the multi-version concurrency-control bookkeeping layer, where obsolete row versions, rollback records, and logically deleted index entries accumulate faster than background cleanup workers can reclaim them. It is distinct from lock contention because the failure mode is version-store growth and visibility-check overhead rather than blocking on lock objects. Observable phenomena: rising ratios of obsolete to live rows reported by table-statistics views, growing version-store or rollback-segment length, increasing physical size of tables and indexes alongside declining live-row density per page, longer sequential scans, planner misestimates caused by the bloated heap, cleanup workers continuously busy or visibly falling behind, and engine warnings about impending transaction-id horizon or version-store wraparound. Possible contributing factors: heavy update and delete churn under page-fill settings that prevent in-place updates, long idle-in-transaction sessions or replication-state objects holding old read snapshots, cleanup worker thresholds and cost limits set too conservatively for the workload, insufficient maintenance memory or I/O budget, large batch deletes without partition rotation, and cleanup workers disabled or under-resourced.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly
Description: Definition: Root cause located at the engine-configuration layer, where runtime parameters governing memory pools, checkpoint cadence, log sizing, background workers, parallelism, isolation, and durability are not calibrated to the hardware capacity, workload mix, or version-specific defaults. It is distinct from the resource layers it controls because the failure originates from the parameter setting itself rather than from the underlying physical resource truly reaching its limit. Observable phenomena: wait-event distribution that does not match hardware utilization, such as heavy log-write waits while the storage device is idle or sustained CPU spinning while cores are not saturated, checkpoint or page-flush storms triggered immediately after a configuration change, background cleanup falling behind despite a low data-modification rate, and workload regressions appearing right after upgrades, instance resizing, or manual tuning. Possible contributing factors: buffer-pool size mismatched to available memory, per-session work memory set too high or too low for the concurrency level, checkpoint-cadence and transaction-log size parameters not aligned with the redo generation rate, cleanup-worker thresholds not aligned with the data-modification rate, parallelism limits over- or under-provisioned for the available cores, connection limits set beyond what per-session memory can sustain, and version-default changes silently altering semantics after upgrades.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly
Description: Definition: Root cause located at the engine memory-allocation layer, where the total amount of physical memory or swap consumed by buffer caches, plan caches, per-session work areas, sort and hash buffers, temporary structures, parallel workers, and background heaps exceeds the safe envelope of the host. It addresses the size and growth of memory regions and is distinct from how efficiently buffer pages are accessed or serialized. Observable phenomena: sustained operating-system memory pressure, paging or swapping activity, out-of-memory termination events, continuous growth of database-process resident-set size, declining cache hit ratios driven by allocation churn, memory-pressure-induced CPU stalls, and node eviction or abnormal restarts in clustered or virtualized deployments. Possible contributing factors: per-query work memory left uncapped and amplified by high concurrency, runaway hash or sort operations materializing in memory, excessive parallel workers each reserving private buffers, plan-cache bloat caused by un-parameterized ad-hoc statements, session leaks or long-lived sessions holding cursor and array state, in-memory column store or result cache mis-sized for the workload, and memory leaks within user-defined functions, extensions, or stored procedures.

Name: Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly
Description: Definition: Root cause located inside the buffer manager, where sessions stall while contending for shared buffer-cache pages, page pins, page-content locks, lightweight synchronization primitives, latches, in-flight I/O slots, or dirty-page flush slots. It sits below transaction-level row and table locks and is distinct from raw memory-size problems because the failure mode is page-level access serialization rather than overall memory exhaustion. Observable phenomena: elevated buffer-busy and page-latch wait events in engine wait-event views, prolonged latch acquisition reported by performance-tracing facilities, CPU spinning without throughput gain, and latency spikes concentrated on hot index root pages, sequence-like pages, or counter rows. Possible contributing factors: hot pages repeatedly accessed by many concurrent sessions, an undersized buffer pool that forces constant page churn, slow storage prolonging dirty-page flush cycles, aggressive checkpoint or background-writer settings, cleanup or bulk-load activity monopolizing buffer I/O, monotonic insert patterns concentrating writes on a single page, and inappropriate latch or spin-loop configuration in highly parallel workloads.

Name: Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description: Definition: Root cause located in the transaction-log subsystem, where the generation, flushing, switching, archiving, or retention of write-ahead log records becomes the bottleneck on the write path. It is distinct from generic storage I/O because the bottleneck is specific to the log-file group, log buffer, archiver process, and replication-retention pipeline rather than to overall device capacity. Observable phenomena: rising commit latency, elevated log-flush, log-write, and log-sync wait events, frequent log-file switches and checkpoint storms reported in engine alert logs, continuously growing log-file and archive directories, archival processes lagging behind the latest log position, and write workloads stalling when the next log segment is unavailable. Possible contributing factors: log files undersized relative to the peak redo generation rate, too few log groups or log segments, log files placed on the same device as busy data or temporary files, log buffer and commit-batching parameters not tuned for the workload, archive destinations slow or full, replication-state objects retaining log segments because downstream consumers are disconnected, and synchronous-commit policies enabled without validating the latency budget.

Name: Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description: Definition: Root cause located in the replication pipeline, where standbys, read replicas, subscribers, or downstream change-data consumers cannot receive, persist, or apply transaction-log records at the rate the primary produces them. It is distinct from the local log subsystem and from storage anomalies because the failure surface is the cross-node receive and apply path rather than the primary's own write path. Observable phenomena: widening log-position gaps reported by replication-state monitoring views, increasing receive, write, flush, and replay lag, growing relay logs or retained primary log segments, stale reads on replicas, reduced failover readiness, and primary-side disk usage growing because replication-state objects prevent log recycling. Possible contributing factors: insufficient network bandwidth or excessive latency between primary and replica, replica CPU or I/O incapable of replaying redo at the source rate, single-threaded or under-parallelized apply processes, oversized transactions or schema-change operations applied as a single unit, schema or index differences between primary and replica, apply-side lock conflicts, replication filtering or conflict-resolution errors, and disconnected or paused consumers whose retention objects remain active.

Name: Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description: Definition: Root cause located in the persisted on-disk data and index structures, where physical pages, key ordering, page links, page checksums, or index-to-heap mappings have become inconsistent with the logical contents of the relations. It is independent of access-path or maintenance anomalies because the underlying structure itself is no longer trustworthy. Observable phenomena: index scans returning missing or duplicated rows, heap-scan counts diverging from index-scan counts, page-checksum or page-verification errors written to engine logs, integrity-verification utilities reporting key-order, leaf-row, or page-link errors, internal assertion failures, sudden plan fallback to full scans for previously index-served queries, and engine-reported physical or logical corruption errors. Possible contributing factors: storage subsystem faults or firmware defects, memory or processor bit flips not caught by error-correction mechanisms, power loss or ungraceful shutdown bypassing write-ahead semantics, engine defects in concurrency or recovery code paths, incomplete crash recovery, failed online index rebuilds, replication or materialized-view replay gaps, and version or storage-format mismatches after upgrades.

Name: Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description: Definition: Root cause located at the storage device or storage-virtualization layer, where the sustained rate of physical reads and writes saturates the throughput, IOPS, or latency budget of the underlying volumes used by data files, temporary files, log files, and backup destinations. It is distinct from the engine-level subsystems that submit I/O because the limiting factor is the physical capacity of the device rather than how the engine is configured. Observable phenomena: device-level wait time well above device service time, sharply rising read and write latency on the underlying volumes, queue depths pegged near their maximum, high database I/O wait while CPU utilization remains moderate, wait profiles dominated by data-file, temporary-file, log-file, buffer-I/O, and durability-flush events, and elongated batch windows and statement response times. Possible contributing factors: insufficient spindle count or insufficient provisioned IOPS, write penalties from the storage layout, asynchronous I/O disabled or filesystem read-ahead too small, mismatch between filesystem block size and database page size, hot data and log files concentrated on a single device, missing flash or solid-state caching tier, virtualization or shared-storage neighbor contention, and storage-controller or path-failure events degrading throughput.

Name: Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description: Definition: Root cause located at the storage capacity dimension, where the physical or logical free space allocated to data files, indexes, tablespaces, transaction logs, archive logs, rollback areas, temporary work areas, backup destinations, or diagnostic logs reaches a hard boundary. It is distinct from I/O throughput anomalies because the failure mode is space exhaustion rather than bandwidth or latency. Observable phenomena: rapidly declining free space, data-file or tablespace auto-extension failures, allocation-failed or no-space errors raised to clients and recorded in engine logs, log and archive destinations becoming full, temporary-space failures during sorts, hash operations, or index builds, backup-area saturation, and cascading stalls when log segments cannot be recycled or archives cannot be written. Possible contributing factors: uncontrolled data growth without retention or partition rotation, burst data-load or replication activity, oversized or orphaned temporary objects and large object payloads, missing log and archive cleanup policies, auto-extension disabled or capped below realistic peak demand, failed maintenance jobs that would normally reclaim space, backup retention silently retaining old sets, and monitoring tied only to percentage thresholds rather than to absolute free space and growth velocity.

Name: CPU Resource Anomaly
Description: Definition: Root cause located at the host CPU resource layer, where database-related processes consume an abnormally large and sustained share of CPU, leaving insufficient cycles for the rest of the workload. It is distinct from query-plan or workload anomalies because the diagnosis target is the saturation of the compute resource itself, regardless of which logical layer originally produced the demand. Observable phenomena: sustained host CPU utilization near saturation, elevated operating-system run queue and load average, increased context-switch rate, scheduler and runqueue wait events appearing in engine wait-event views, top statements concentrated by CPU time, and broad latency increases across otherwise unrelated statements once cores become saturated. Possible contributing factors: aggregate effect of inefficient queries, plan regressions, or missing indexes converging on CPU usage, excessive parallelism producing context-switch thrashing, maintenance or bulk-load jobs overlapping peak traffic, bind-value-sensitive plan reuse keeping a CPU-intensive plan in cache, tight application polling and connection-leak-driven active result sets, co-located services or noisy-neighbor virtual machines sharing physical cores, and undersized compute capacity relative to workload growth.

Name: Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description: Definition: Root cause located at the operating-system kernel and per-process resource-limit layer, where database processes, sessions, or background workers exhaust limits enforced by the host kernel rather than by the database engine itself. It is distinct from database memory, CPU, storage, and network anomalies because the limiting resource is a kernel-managed object such as file handles, shared memory segments, semaphores, message queues, asynchronous-I/O contexts, process or thread quotas, virtual address ranges, or namespace and cgroup quotas. Observable phenomena: engine errors referring to inability to open files, allocate shared memory, create threads, or acquire kernel synchronization primitives, kernel-reported denials of resource allocation visible in system message logs, intermittent failures of new sessions or background workers despite database-level slots being available, sudden inability to spawn parallel workers, and partial outages where the engine continues to serve existing work but cannot expand. Possible contributing factors: overly conservative per-process file-handle, locked-memory, or stack-size limits, kernel-level shared-memory or semaphore caps left at default values, virtual-memory or address-space configuration insufficient for the engine footprint, asynchronous-I/O context limits saturated by parallel workers, process or thread quotas reached after connection bursts, container or cgroup memory and process-id limits reached, and orphaned resources (handles, shared segments, semaphores) accumulating after abnormal terminations.

Name: Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description: Definition: Root cause located in the network and connection-handling layer between clients and the database server, where transport, transport-security, listener, authentication, socket I/O, or connection-slot resources cannot service the offered request rate. It is distinct from in-engine waits because the bottleneck lies in cross-host data movement and connection lifecycle rather than in statement execution. Observable phenomena: client-visible connection-establishment timeouts and connection-class error codes, increasing counters of aborted or refused connections, accumulation of half-open or wait-state sockets at the operating-system layer, established sessions accumulating client-read or client-write wait events, too-many-connections rejections with backend process or thread counts at the configured limit, oversized result sets holding backends idle while bytes are sent, and elevated network retransmission and round-trip-time metrics correlated with database latency. Possible contributing factors: network congestion, packet loss, asymmetric path size, deep firewall or application-layer proxy inspection, name-resolution or reverse-lookup delay, listener backlog and operating-system socket queue limits set too small, exhausted server-side processes or threads stalling authentication, oversized application connection pools or connection leaks, retry storms after brief outages, large result-set transfers and slow client consumers, transport-security handshake overhead, and intermediate network devices resetting idle sockets.
